questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Identify which DNA strand is copied during transcription and what the transcript matches
questions.stem: In her 8 January observing log, Rosa used the idea of a template and a tracing to describe two strands of a gene. Which statement about the template and coding strands is correct?

options.text: The RNA transcript matches the coding strand in sequence, with uracil replacing every thymine.
Both strands are copied at once, so one gene can make two different transcripts in opposite directions.
options.misconception: believes both strands are transcribed at the same time

options.text: The coding strand is the one copied by the enzyme, so the transcript is complementary to the coding strand.
options.misconception: confuses which strand the polymerase copies

options.text: The template strand has the same sequence as the transcript, but it carries thymine in place of uracil.
options.misconception: assumes the transcript matches the template strand

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase reads the template and builds a complementary transcript, so the RNA matches the coding strand with U for T. The trap is calling the coding strand the one that gets copied.
questions.hint: Ask which strand the polymerase physically reads.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Use exon and intron lengths to work out the size of a mature message
questions.stem: Entry for 19 February, cold and clear: the log tabulates one pre-messenger RNA as exon A of 180, exon B of 240, intron 1 of 310 and intron 2 of 95 nucleotides. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The mature message contains 180 + 310 + 240 + 95 = 825 nucleotides once the parts are joined.
options.misconception: adds the introns into the final transcript

options.text: The mature message contains 310 + 95 = 405 nucleotides, since only the removed pieces survive.
options.misconception: keeps the introns and discards the exons

options.text: The mature message contains 180 + 240 = 420 nucleotides, because introns are removed during processing.
The mature message contains all 825 nucleotides, since splicing only adds a cap and a tail.
options.misconception: thinks splicing changes length without removing anything

questions.explanation: Exons are retained and introns are cut out, so the mature RNA is 180 + 240 = 420 nucleotides. The trap is adding or keeping the introns, which never reach the ribosome.
questions.hint: Ask which pieces survive splicing.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the number of transcript variants from a set of optional exons
questions.stem: A 3 March entry records that one gene gave rise to several mature transcripts by choosing different exon combinations, and the observer asks how many distinct messages are possible if each of three exons is either included or skipped independently.
questions.explanation: Each of the three exons has two independent states, so the number of combinations is 2 x 2 x 2 = 8. Adding the choices instead of multiplying them would give 6, which is wrong.
questions.hint: Think of each exon as an on or off switch.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Why No Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why transcription can begin without a primer
questions.stem: While the mount was tracking Saturn, Mira wondered why the enzyme that copies DNA into RNA can begin without a primer, unlike the enzyme that copies DNA. Explain why no primer is required for transcription.

answer.exemplar: RNA polymerase can start a transcript on its own because it binds directly to promoter DNA, melts a short bubble of the double helix and positions the first free ribonucleotides itself, whereas DNA polymerase can only extend an existing chain by adding to a free 3' hydroxyl group. A DNA primer must therefore be made first, while transcription needs none.

questions.explanation: The transcriptase recognises the promoter and starts a chain itself, so no pre-existing 3' end is needed. DNA polymerase can only extend an existing chain end, which is why it requires a primer.
questions.hint: Think about where the enzyme first binds.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a diagram of the enzyme that loads an amino acid onto a transfer RNA
questions.stem: The 22 April page of the log shows a sketch with three boxes joined in a row, labelled amino acid, transfer RNA and enzyme, with an arrow from the amino acid into the enzyme and a second arrow leaving the enzyme towards the transfer RNA. What does the diagram show?

options.text: The enzyme breaks the transfer RNA into two short strands and releases the amino acid again.
options.misconception: thinks the enzyme destroys the transfer RNA

options.text: The transfer RNA delivers its amino acid to the enzyme, which then folds the RNA into a loop.
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the charging step

options.text: The enzyme attaches the correct amino acid to the transfer RNA, using the anticodon to identify it.
The amino acid is transferred onto the growing chain and the empty transfer RNA is released.
options.misconception: confuses charging with the elongation step

questions.explanation: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase matches each anticodon to its amino acid and links the two, giving a charged transfer RNA. The error is to confuse this loading step with delivery at the ribosome.
questions.hint: Follow the arrows from the amino acid.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Spot an error in a claim that links an anticodon to the wrong codon
questions.stem: A failed observation on 6 May left time for writing, and the note claims that a transfer RNA carrying methionine pairs with the codon GUU because both spell out valine in some tables. Identify the error in this reasoning.

options.text: The error is that the anticodon must be written with T instead of U so that it matches the codon exactly.
options.misconception: believes anticodons are written with thymine

options.text: The error is that pairing must be identical base for base with no wobble allowed at the third position.
options.misconception: denies wobble at the third codon position

options.text: The error is that the anticodon for AUG is CAU, and GUU is read by a different transfer RNA carrying valine.
The error is that methionine is the only amino acid whose codon also codes for valine in the table.
options.misconception: invents overlapping codon meanings

questions.explanation: AUG, not GUU, is the methionine codon, and its anticodon is CAU with the usual wobble at the third base. GUU codes for valine and is read by a different transfer RNA entirely.
questions.hint: Check the codon table entry for methionine.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment that tracks a transfer RNA through the ribosome sites
questions.stem: After rain washed the dust off the mirror, the log asks how an experiment could show where a transfer RNA sits at each stage of translation. Describe an experiment using a labelled transfer RNA and the ribosome.

answer.exemplar: Add a synthetic messenger RNA of defined sequence and a fluorescently labelled transfer RNA to a cell-free ribosome mixture, then follow the label through assembly using a microscope or a gel filtration column. Repeating the run with transfer RNAs of different chain lengths or modified bases reveals which site holds the growing chain, which receives the arriving transfer RNA, and which releases the empty one.

questions.explanation: Tracking a labelled transfer RNA as the ribosome cycles through its three sites shows the arrival, peptidyl and exit positions in turn. Without a labelled handle, positions can only be inferred.
questions.hint: You need a handle that follows one transfer RNA.

questions.topic: Information Flow: The Usual Direction and Its Exception
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a case in which information flows from RNA back into DNA
questions.stem: Midnight, 19 June: the log notes that information usually runs from DNA to RNA to protein, and asks about the exception to that rule. Which case best shows information flowing in the reverse direction?

options.text: A cell copies its whole genome so that a daughter cell can repair a broken chromosome.
options.misconception: calls DNA replication a reversal of information flow

options.text: A cell makes many identical copies of one messenger RNA before it is used or degraded.
options.misconception: treats messenger RNA copies as reverse information flow

options.text: A cell reads the sequence of a protein to decide which genes to switch on during division.
options.misconception: believes protein sequences are read back into DNA

options.text: An enzyme copies the sequence of an RNA template back into DNA, as retroviruses do.

questions.explanation: Reverse transcription makes DNA from an RNA template, so information moves from RNA back to DNA. Replication and transcript amplification copy DNA or RNA forwards and are not exceptions.
questions.hint: Look for a case where RNA is the starting template.

questions.learningObjective: Use a pair of written strands and a transcript to identify the coding strand
questions.stem: In the July section of the notebook, the writer notes two antiparallel strands of a gene, the first running 5' to 3' as ACGTTGCA and the second running 3' to 5' as TGCAACGT, and a transcript reading 5' ACGUUGCA 3'. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The first strand is the template strand, since it is the one written with a 5' end.
options.misconception: assumes the left-listed strand must be the template

options.text: Both strands serve as templates, producing two identical transcripts in opposite directions.
options.misconception: believes both strands are copied at once

options.text: The second strand is the template strand, and the transcript matches the first strand with U for T.
Neither strand can be copied, because the two sequences shown are complementary to one another.
options.misconception: thinks complementary strands cannot be transcribed

questions.explanation: The transcript reads ACGUUGCA, so it matches the first strand with U for T, making that the coding strand and the second the template. The classic error is to assume the first strand is the template.
questions.hint: Compare the transcript with each strand.

questions.stem: A note written on a train to the star party says the pre-messenger RNA measured that evening contained 1500 nucleotides, including three introns of 260, 340 and 180 nucleotides. How many nucleotides remain in the mature messenger RNA?

questions.learningObjective: Interpret a gene sketch that shows two products from one gene
questions.stem: The 2 September entry, in a shakier hand, records a sketch of a gene with four numbered exons and a bracket drawn across the middle of exon 2, plus two arrows from the same gene to two different mature strands. What does the diagram show?

options.text: One gene is cut into two genes, and each half is then copied into a separate messenger RNA.
options.misconception: thinks the gene itself is duplicated

options.text: Two different promoters start the same gene, producing transcripts with different first exons.
options.misconception: confuses alternative splicing with alternative promoters

options.text: Two versions of exon 2 are made by editing the bases of the message after it leaves the nucleus.
options.misconception: moves RNA editing into splicing

options.text: One gene yields two messenger RNAs by joining exons in different combinations.

questions.explanation: Two arrows to two mature strands from one gene with a bracketed variable exon is the signature of alternative splicing. Confusing it with promoter choice or RNA editing misses the exon joining step.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Why No Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: Correct a flawed explanation of why transcription needs no primer
questions.stem: Before packing the 3 October gear, the observer wrote that RNA polymerase must be handed a short starter stretch because, in the writer's words, nothing can be made without a template. State what is wrong with this reasoning.

options.text: The error is that the promoter is a protein rather than a stretch of DNA at which the enzyme binds.
options.misconception: thinks the promoter is a protein molecule

options.text: The error is that the DNA duplex itself is the template; the promoter simply marks where to start.
The error is that a primer is needed only for RNA and never for DNA, so the rule is backwards.
options.misconception: reverses which polymerase needs a primer

options.text: The error is that transcription can only begin at the very start of a chromosome, not at a promoter.
options.misconception: assumes promoters sit only at chromosome ends

questions.explanation: The DNA duplex is the template the polymerase copies, and the promoter is simply the DNA sequence that says where to begin. No separate primer is needed because the enzyme starts a chain itself.
questions.hint: Separate the template from the start signal.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why amino acids are attached to transfer RNA by a separate enzyme
questions.stem: At a cloudy night in November, the observer used the waiting time to write why the cell needs a dedicated enzyme to attach amino acids to transfer RNA. Explain why charging is done by an enzyme rather than by the ribosome.

answer.exemplar: Each transfer RNA must carry exactly the amino acid that its anticodon specifies, and the cell guarantees this with aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases, which recognise the amino acid and the transfer RNA together and can edit a wrongly loaded one. The ribosome only checks codon and anticodon pairing and would happily use a mischarged transfer RNA, so loading and proofreading must happen before assembly.

questions.explanation: Correct charging needs an enzyme that recognises the anticodon and the amino acid together and can proofread the match. The ribosome only tests pairing, so it cannot correct a mischarged transfer RNA.
questions.hint: Think about which step checks accuracy.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: State the correct relationship between a codon and its anticodon
questions.stem: A folded page from December explains that the anticodon of a transfer RNA reads a codon by pairing antiparallel. Which statement about this pairing is correct?

options.text: The anticodon is the reverse complement of the codon, read 3' to 5' against a 5' to 3' codon.
The anticodon has the same sequence as the codon, just written in the opposite direction.
options.misconception: treats anticodon and codon as identical sequences

options.text: The anticodon pairs with the template strand of DNA rather than with the codon in the message.
options.misconception: pairs the anticodon with DNA instead of RNA

options.text: The anticodon is written with thymine so that it can pair with the adenine of the codon.
options.misconception: thinks anticodons contain thymine

questions.explanation: Antiparallel pairing means the anticodon is the reverse complement of the codon, with C pairing G and A pairing U. Reading it in the same direction as the codon is the usual source of confusion.
questions.hint: Draw both strands 5' to 3' and see.

questions.learningObjective: Assign ribosome sites from a record of where transfer RNAs are found
questions.stem: One January night, with the dome frozen, the log tabulates where three transfer RNAs sat: t1 in the middle position while holding the growing chain, t2 in the side position receiving the new amino acid, and t3 in the third position empty. Which set of names is correct?

options.text: The middle position is the A site, the side position is the P site, and the empty one is the exit site.
options.misconception: confuses the arrival site with the chain-holding site

options.text: The middle position is the P site, the side position is the E site, and the empty one is the A site.
options.misconception: assigns the exit site to the arrival position

options.text: The middle position is the E site, the side position is the P site, and the empty one is the A site.
options.misconception: puts the empty site where the chain is held

options.text: The middle position is the P site, the side position is the A site, and the empty one is the E site.

questions.explanation: The peptidyl site holds the chain, the arrival site receives the new transfer RNA, and the exit site releases the empty one. Swapping the arrival and peptidyl names is the classic mistake.
questions.hint: The site holding the chain keeps the same name.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a helix sketch showing polymerase travel and chain direction
questions.stem: The notebook's first entry this year notes a sketch of a double helix drawn as two parallel lines with 5' and 3' labels at the ends, a polymerase blob on the lower line and an arrow showing it moving left to right, with the lower line labelled 3' on the left and 5' on the right. options.text: It travels along the lower strand from 3' to 5' while extending the new chain toward the left.
options.misconception: reverses the direction in which the chain grows

options.text: It travels along the lower strand from 5' to 3' while building the transcript toward the right.
options.misconception: assumes the chain grows opposite to the enzyme travel

options.text: It travels along the template strand from 3' to 5', building the transcript 5' to 3'.

options.misconception: has the enzyme and transcript travelling together

questions.learningObjective: Correct a description that reverses the roles of introns and exons
questions.stem: After the alignment stars vanished, the log records a visitant's claim that introns are the parts of a gene that are kept in the final message and exons are the parts cut away. Identify what is wrong with this description.

options.misconception: claims introns are the retained parts

options.misconception: treats the terms as unrelated molecules

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how one gene can be read to make more than one protein
questions.stem: A sunny afternoon spent sorting eyepieces, the writer explains why one gene can give rise to several protein versions. Explain how alternative splicing produces more than one protein from a single gene.

answer.exemplar: Alternative splicing lets the cell join the same set of exons in more than one permitted pattern, so different mature transcripts are made from one gene. Each transcript is then translated into a different protein because the amino acids included change and the reading frame can shift. This expands the number of products a fixed genome can make without new genes, and the pattern chosen can depend on the cell type or its conditions.

questions.explanation: Joining exons in different patterns gives different mature transcripts, each read into a different protein. The error is to think only exons, never introns, vary between products.
questions.hint: Focus on which exons are joined together.

options.text: RNA polymerase starts a chain at a promoter by itself, whereas DNA polymerase needs an existing 3' end.

questions.explanation: RNA polymerase recognises the promoter, opens the duplex and starts a chain itself, so no primer is needed. DNA polymerase can only extend an existing chain end, which is why it requires one.
questions.hint: Ask what each enzyme needs at the start.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Information Flow: The Usual Direction and Its Exception
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a virus can copy its genetic material back into DNA
questions.stem: Combing through the old floppy discs, the writer explains a case in which information runs backwards through the cell. Explain how a virus can copy its genetic material back into DNA.

answer.exemplar: Some viruses carry their genome as RNA and an enzyme called reverse transcriptase. That enzyme uses the viral RNA as a template and synthesises a complementary DNA strand, which then serves as template for a second DNA strand, forming a double-stranded copy that can be inserted into the host genome. Information therefore flows from RNA to DNA, opposite to the usual DNA to RNA to protein route.

questions.explanation: Reverse transcriptase copies RNA into DNA, so the flow of information runs against the usual direction. Treating this as ordinary transcription or replication misses that the template is RNA.
questions.hint: Name the enzyme that reads RNA and writes DNA.

questions.learningObjective: Design an experiment that identifies which DNA strand serves as a template
questions.stem: On a clear February night, Ilse wrote that the two strands of a DNA molecule can each carry genes, and asked how one could find out which strand is used as the template for a particular gene. Describe the experiment.

answer.exemplar: Make a labelled copy of the messenger RNA made from the gene, then let it pair with each of the two DNA strands in turn and extend. The template strand is complementary to the RNA and will support extension, while the coding strand carries the same sequence as the RNA and will not, so the reaction that makes new material identifies the template.

questions.explanation: The template is complementary to the transcript, so only one strand can pair with the RNA and act as a template. Reading a test that shows both strands pairing misidentifies the roles.
questions.hint: Ask which strand pairs with the RNA.

answer.exemplar: RNA polymerase recognises a promoter sequence in the DNA, separates the two strands at that spot and positions the first nucleotides itself, so it can begin a transcript with no starter strand. answer.exemplar: Introns are sequences that are transcribed but not needed for the mature message, so the cell removes them with a splicing machinery that cuts the RNA at defined boundaries and joins the exon ends together. questions.learningObjective: Correct a claim that splicing adds exons to the message
questions.stem: Two decades of observing later, the observer finds a mistake in an old entry that claimed alternative splicing adds extra exons to the messenger RNA. Identify what is wrong with that entry.

options.text: The error is that splicing adds nucleotides to the messenger RNA rather than removing them.
options.misconception: believes splicing adds sequence

options.text: The error is that splicing only removes pieces; it never adds exons that the gene lacks.
The error is that alternative splicing happens in the cytoplasm rather than in the nucleus.
options.misconception: misplaces the compartment

options.text: The error is that the discarded pieces are kept and rejoined at the end of the message.
options.misconception: thinks introns are relocated

questions.explanation: Splicing removes introns and joins the exons that the gene already contains, so it can change the combination but never add new exons. The entry's claim would require sequence to appear from nowhere.
questions.hint: Ask whether any new sequence appears.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.topic: Transcription: Why No Primer Is Needed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why only one of the two copying enzymes needs a primer
questions.stem: Fog again on the second weekend, so the log ends with a visitor's question: why does copying DNA need a primer when copying a gene into RNA does not? Explain the difference.

answer.exemplar: DNA polymerase cannot begin a chain from nothing; it can only add a nucleotide to the free 3' hydroxyl group already present on a strand, so a primer must be supplied, usually a short RNA made by a dedicated enzyme. RNA polymerase recognises a promoter sequence in the DNA, melts the duplex there, positions the first nucleotides itself and starts a transcript, so it needs no primer. The difference lies in how the two enzymes initiate synthesis.

questions.explanation: One enzyme can start a chain on bare DNA while the other can only extend an existing chain end, which is why one needs a primer. Claiming both behave alike, or that the DNA end supplies it, is wrong.
questions.hint: Compare how each enzyme initiates.
